# Chapter exercise: Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na {.unnumbered}

**Which North Carolina Airport Has the Worst Delays?**

This exercise goes with **Chapter 8, Into the Tidyverse: summarize, group_by, and drop_na**. It builds on the Chapter 6 and 7 exercises, and uses the same flights to North Carolina. It should take you about **one hour**. Read this whole section before you start.

## Purpose

**Skills you'll practice.** By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

1. Collapse a data frame into summary statistics with `summarize()`, using `mean()`, `median()`, `sd()`, `max()`, and `n()`.
2. Calculate the same statistics for each group with `group_by()` and `summarize()`, and count groups with `count()`.
3. Group by two columns, and know when a result is still grouped.
4. Handle missing values on purpose, with `na.rm = TRUE`, `sum(is.na())`, or `drop_na()`, and explain how they differ.
5. Tell an average of averages from a weighted average, and calculate the weighted one.

**Knowledge you'll gain.** You'll compare delays and cancellations at North Carolina's five airports, find out which airlines were most often late, and see how much the "average speed" of a route depends on how you average it.

**Why this matters.** Most numbers in a report are summaries: the median income of a county, the average commute in a state, the rate of a disease in a region. `group_by()` and `summarize()` make those numbers for every place at once, and they are how you'll turn tract data into county data later in the course. Choosing between a mean and a median, deciding what to do with missing values, and weighting an average correctly are the judgment calls that make a summary honest.

## Task

Work through Parts 1 to 7 in order, top to bottom. In each part:

- Read the short explanation, then do each step marked with a bullet (•).
- Wherever you see `___`, replace it with the missing code **before** you run the chunk. A chunk with `___` in it won't run.
- **Before you run** each chunk, predict how many rows it will return. Then run it and check.
- Answer each question (**Q1**, **Q2**, ...) in a sentence or two of Markdown, where it says *Your answer here.*
- Give every summary column a name, as in `summarize(mean_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))`.

| Part | What you'll do | About |
|:-----|:---------------|:------|
| 1 | Set up your file and keep the flights to North Carolina | 3 min |
| 2 | Summarize every flight with `summarize()` | 8 min |
| 3 | One result per airport and airline with `group_by()` | 15 min |
| 4 | Group by two columns | 8 min |
| 5 | Missing values: `na.rm`, `is.na()`, and `drop_na()` | 10 min |
| 6 | The average of averages | 12 min |
| 7 | Reflect, knit, and turn in | 4 min |

**Turn in** your `.Rmd` file and your knitted `.html` file on Canvas.

## Criteria for success

Use this checklist before you turn your work in. Each item matches a row of the rubric below.

- [ ] The file knits to HTML with no errors, and the author and date at the top are yours.
- [ ] Every `___` has been filled in, and every chunk runs.
- [ ] Every question (Q1 to Q11) has an answer in complete sentences.
- [ ] Answers that ask for a statistic say which statistic it is (mean or median), give its units, and name the group it belongs to.
- [ ] Every column made in `summarize()` has a clear, snake_case name.
- [ ] Every chain uses the pipe `|>`, with one step per line.
- [ ] No `install.packages()` line is anywhere in the file.
- [ ] The three reflection questions are answered.

| Criterion | Full credit | Partial credit | No credit |
|:----------|:------------|:---------------|:----------|
| Knits (2 pts) | Knits to HTML with no errors | Knits, but some chunks have errors shown | Doesn't knit, or no HTML turned in |
| Code (6 pts) | Every blank filled in correctly; every chunk returns what was asked | Most blanks correct | Many blanks missing or wrong |
| Questions (8 pts) | Q1 to Q11 answered correctly, using the output, with units and reasons | Some answers missing, wrong, or with no reason | Most answers missing |
| Weighted average (2 pts) | Part 6 calculates both averages and explains why they differ | Calculates both, but doesn't explain | Not done |
| Style (1 pt) | Named summary columns, pipe for every chain, one step per line, no `install.packages()` | | Several problems |
| Reflection (1 pt) | All three answered | | Missing |

**What a good answer looks like.** Here is a question, a weak answer, and a strong one.

> *Question:* How late were flights from New York in 2013, on average?
>
> *Weak answer:* "12.6."
>
> *Strong answer:* "The mean departure delay was 12.6 minutes, but the median was −2 minutes: more than half of the flights left early. A few very long delays pull the mean up, so the median is the better 'typical' delay."

The strong answer names the statistic and its units, compares the mean with the median, and says which one describes a typical flight.

**IMPORTANT!** Save often. Before you knit, choose **Run > Restart R and Run All Chunks** to make sure every chunk works from a fresh start.
